utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Andrew Cayley, assisted by Lise-Lotte Karlsson this afternoon. Good afternoon; Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Ms. Korner. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with my co-counsel Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Ackerman. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. I understand there are some preliminaries. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour. Mr. McLeod did work over the weekend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I hand to Your Honours -- or have you already been handed it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: His revised typed version based on his own reading of the notes. The Defence have just got it. And there's one for the registry as well. And if necessary, if the interpreters require it, we can hand out copies. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, there has been one more glitch, I'm afraid, in the witnesses. Witness number 33 on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With the number 7.119.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was due to testify one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One after the next, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When he was contacted by VWS he told them that he'd just got a job after a very long time of being unemployed to start this Monday and asked if his testimony could be put back. So we said it could. I don't think it matters much. We estimate we have enough to fill up the rest of the week anyhow because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the important thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And please keep in mind that this week we are not sitting on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Exactly. So we've got two more witnesses lined up for this week, and we estimate that number 34, 7.59, will take a little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So actually we're talking of 7.112.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 7.112 either -- later this afternoon or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then followed by 7.59.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I just tell Your Honours in advance that 7.59 does have medical problems. He was the one we were worried about. But he's attended. But just to forewarn Your Honour that there may be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's good to forewarn us, definitely. I think what we ought to do is -- Madam Registrar, I don't know what the practice has been so far, whether it's the Prosecution that does this or whether it's the Registry, to alert the Victims and Witnesses Section to be on standby, should there be an emergency. I mean, that's very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it's a long-standing illness, but he's been receiving treatment for it recently and I'm just alerting the Court of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner. And when I say to be alerted, to remain on standby, it doesn't mean only while he's giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Afterwards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While -- during his entire stay here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. Mr. Ackerman or any preliminaries? There is a couple of things that I need to mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the proposed schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: From now to the end of the year either prepared and presented to the Prosecutor. They will obviously go through it in good time, and it will be in your hands by the middle of the week I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And also I'll try to communicate to you one particular week where we need a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask -- if Your Honour would assist, it would help us by simply letting us know what days you, as the Trial Chamber, won't be sitting. That would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. I mean, I personally need to be away -- I need to be in Malta on the 16th of November for sure. So that's 16th of November is a Saturday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Saturday. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I need to be in Malta one or two days before that. That's the only --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour, that would help. And if we could know in advance also what days are set aside for court maintenance or plenaries or things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have asked my secretary to inquire into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems to be alternating -- seems to be a practice they alternate one courtroom after another one Friday and then it's one other Friday in a month which is skipped entirely. So that's -- but she's going to find out for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The trouble is we seem to move courtrooms and then move into the courtroom that has maintenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you it's -- I have nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. It's just unfortunate. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, there are just a couple of minor things that I needed to bring to your attention, and one is due to the fact that we have six trials ongoing on any given day here and some of us have got either Status Conferences to attend to or Pre-Trial Conferences or whatever. Unfortunately on the 23rd of next month, of -- the 23rd of next month, on July, in other words, which will be a Tuesday - yeah - I will be holding a Status Conference and I have to hold it at 2.15 p.m. In other words, we will have to take one hour from Brdjanin and Talic on that particular day in order to be able to sit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we're in the mornings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We are in the afternoon. In July, we are in the afternoon as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, are we? All right. I thought we were switching to the mornings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I hope. I hope we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thought I saw on the list that we were back to a morning sitting, but I may be wrong on that. In July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I haven't got the July one here, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have it and it shows afternoons. It shows a sitting at 2.15 on July 23rd in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just -- I was in duty bound to alert you to this. I do not expect that Status Conference to last long, also because practically all that needed to be discussed has been already discussed. And it's only a question of a decision pending which will follow hopefully within a week after that. But we will probably need to take one hour from Brdjanin and Talic, and I'm also informed that we would need -- if it's broadcast, if the Status Conference is broadcast, we need an extra 30 minutes then for the room to be prepared. So if there are any changes, I will let you know. The other thing is my attention has been drawn to something that goes back in time to about a month and a half if not two ago. And you will recall, Ms. Korner, that you had made a -- an oral motion regarding filing of -- under Rule 92 bis of statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Made by 7.139 that has been superseded because 7.139 gave evidence last week, and 7.35, who is a witness related to Prijedor. 7.139 was the witness who gave evidence last week --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Re the garage --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes., I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other one is 7.35. And Madam Fauveau had filed a -- a response to that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to think why it would be Prijedor, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was Prijedor. 7.139 was definitely Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't have the motion with me. But I would be surprised because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Relating to this municipality, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think it related to Prijedor, if I am not mistaken, because the occasion was that this witness was -- I think he has already given evidence in the Stakic case. And the idea was that he would give evidence in this case --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then something cropped up. He refused to stay here and give evidence or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. It's coming back to me now, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had suggested that we could postpone -- postpone this, and in the meantime there was the suggestion of filing his testimony under -- under the -- either his testimony or his statement under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: His testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And actually, I had even prepared a draft decision, which is still somewhere in my -- in my -- on my hard disk. But then that's because in anticipation of his coming over while he was giving -- to give evidence while he was giving evidence in the Stakic case. But what I had prepared was entirely restricted to his statement, not to his testimony. Then we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, can we say obviously Prijedor we anticipate should start with all the gaps and dates and delays but sometime in September, and we'll be filing a separate motion. Your Honour, in fact we should be filing this afternoon the -- if I get away to sign it or read it, the Rule 92 motion in respect of the witnesses for Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think we'll do another separate one for Prijedor. And if you could leave that witness till then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. But the reason why I'm raising this issue is that there is already a reply from Madam Fauveau. And basically unless the -- there is something new coming, we would need to decide on this, unless you tell us that this witness will be coming over to give evidence, if you can convince him to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. And once more, I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the witness, if you remember, that has written books or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, firstly, it was done on the basis of -- I think you're right -- of his statement, and it won't be the statement we're seeking to tender it will be the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it seems to me that -- and Your Honour, it may well be that in order to have his evidence admitted, we'd have to do some editing of the transcript from some of the things he said. So I think it would be better if Your Honour were just to regard our original motion as withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we'll refile at a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less that puts Madam Fauveau --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in a situation where she knows where she stands. I'm addressing Madam Fauveau and not you because this is something that she dealt with. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The other thing -- one moment. One other thing is -- but you did mention it now. I was going to remind you today if you had intentions with regard to 92 because of the 21-day period limitation that we had established previously. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may not get filed this afternoon, because I've been in court all day, but it will get filed tomorrow at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to take us into private session for just a moment and tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- something in the role of messenger basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who's going first? Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for keeping you waiting, but we had some preliminaries -- procedural preliminaries that we had to attend to. So please accept the apologies of the Trial Chamber. Could I ask you to proceed with repeating the solemn declaration that you entered last Friday, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. You're now going to be cross-examined by the first of the two Defence teams, and that's Mr. John Ackerman for Radoslav Brdjanin. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One thing I learned over the weekend is you've been through this a number of times, and so I don't think you require much instruction from me with regard to what this is all about, in terms of cross-examination. I want to just go into your background for just a second and very briefly. How long were you in the British army?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't tell us why you left the army. Can you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I resigned my position because I was working in Northern Ireland and realised that the issues that we were dealing with there were more political than military and therefore perhaps I'd be better off doing something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's direct. Thank you. I've gone through in some detail the reports that you wrote about your trips to Northern Bosnia and the ones we discussed during your direct examination here, and what I'd like to know is if you have a fully independent recollection of the matters that are described in those reports or if you can remember those things in the detail you do simply because you have the reports that you can refer to and your notes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends how much detail you want to go down to. I can certainly remember making the trips. I can remember most of what I saw. If you want a verbatim understanding of what was going on in each of the conversations, I certainly can't remember that ten years later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Conversation details would certainly be difficult if you didn't have the notes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You have referred to various people you talked to, Predrag Radic, the gentleman you spoke to in Bosanska Gradiska, and Mr. Stakic. I think you've referred to them all as mayors. In fact, in -- in the government system that was in effect in that area at the time, they were actually presidents of municipalities, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we understood that they were mayors. If there's a difference, then I'm sure there are other people who can sort that out. But they were the individuals that we were speaking to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your mind, you remember speaking to mayors; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my mind, I was speaking to the people who were responsible for those areas, be they governors of municipalities or mayors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That fair. I'd like to go first to your very first meeting in Banja Luka with Mr. Radic. I think that's Exhibit P841.1, and it's the meeting of 23 August 1992. I think you have it there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was the choice made to speak with Mr. Radic? Do you know the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had been one of the main interlocutors that the ECMM had been dealing with before they left Northern Bosnia and therefore he was the first point of contact that ECMM wanted to go back to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So he was a known quantity to ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that -- was that contact with him made by you or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please. Would the counsel make a pause before asking the question so the interpreters can catch up with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness did not have his earphones on. So the interpreters are drawing attention to the fact that you're both English speaking and therefore you just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We need to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You just follow question -- answer follows question immediately and they're not having enough pause in between. So please take care of that, because it -- it will cause unnecessary problems for the interpreters. Mr. Ackerman, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that contact with Mr. Radic to set up that meeting made by you or by someone else in the organisation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was made by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that the initial contact was made and the initial contacts with him were made?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we have looked at earlier on the permissions, the passes that were faxed back and forth, and so I think that would be the record that I would go back to to understand when it was that we'd made contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've not asked my question in a way that you could understand me, so I'll try it again. You spoke about the reason he was the one that was contacted was because on prior visits to Banja Luka, he had been the contact person. And I'm wondering if you know when those prior visits were, when the mission was actually operating there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without having specific dates, the mission had been operating in Northern Bosnia up until the point when the conflict in Bosnia erupted and the mission had then left. But I couldn't give you exact dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Back to this day of 23 August 1992, when you met with Mr. Radic. He had an agenda and he spoke first, I take it, and one of the things that he mentioned - and I think the first thing, according to your report - was that he was concerned about Serb prisoners being health in Rascani and no one being allowed to see them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he asked you to look into that matter.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went back the second time, just a few days later on the 25th of August - two days later, actually - you indicated to Mr. Radic that ECMM had tasked a team to go to Rascani and actually look into the matter that he'd requested that you look into; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Rascani?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we want to use this to identify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can use that if you'd like, yes. It might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this map identifies Tomislavgrad by that name, because they were known by different names. Basically it's in the area in South-West Bosnia, if that would do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be the nearest town that we would all recognise do you think?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Tomislavgrad, if somebody knows the other name by which Tomislavgrad is known by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Livno.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Livno. Okay. Thank you. So in the Livno area. And then Rascani was further, I think, north-west from Livno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you find Livno on the map? Okay. We've got a new name how about Duvno?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It might be quicker if counsel took a map and identified it for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have Duvno. See if that is any use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we've found it. Right? I see Livno. Right under your pen.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see what I'm indicating, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're indicating Livno, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any way to get the map in a little better focus, I wonder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And he is indicating Duvno now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. There we go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And at the time that was called Tomislavgrad apparently? After that. Okay. All right. Thank you. Did a team actually go there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on that occasion the team went into Tomislavgrad, and I think on a subsequent occasion we actually put a team up into Rascani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is Rascani a village or a -- a facility or what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it's a village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was a prison there or something?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that the population was being held in the village, as opposed to being held in a prison. But it was a village, and the village was cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the findings that were made by that team were reported to Mr. Radic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also -- he also asked about as many as 2.000 Serbs that were being held in a tunnel at Bradina. Do you know if a team ever investigated that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think -- I think the ICRC were aware of it. I'm not sure at this distance whether we actually had a team that went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever learn about a place called Celebici?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In your -- during your second meeting -- and I'm looking at page 10 of your report, actually. The indication there is that you got the impression that all of the talk from Mr. Radic about these Serb prisoners was motivated by pressure from families trying to get information regarding relatives or loved ones. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- you're referring to my comment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was fair to say that all the parties at whatever level that you spoke to people were desperately keen to know what was happening to people who were being held on each of the sides by each of the other parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Another concern that was expressed to you during that first meeting by Mr. Radic was that aid was not being allowed to be flown into Banja Luka. And what he said to you was the UN would not allow aid to be flown into Banja Luka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you point me in the right direction in my note, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will. It's on page 1, the last paragraph of your first report, 841.1.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that you'll find -- I can't put my finger on it, but I can certainly remember that further on during the conversations they also make the point that the air space is not being made available by the other two parties. So yes, I think he was making that point, but I think they also make the point that the airport was functional but the other two parties, either Croats and I guess the Muslims, weren't allowing them to use the air space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's also mentioned. You're right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke with Mr. Zupljanin, he also pleaded for your help in getting the airport open, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was a common theme which came up with everybody that we were talking to at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you were trying to re-establish a mission there, the thing that you were interested in was the freedom of movement that you would have in the area of Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these -- these two things we've discussed that Mr. Radic raised with you, he also spoke about the problems of electricity. Was there electricity in Banja Luka when you were there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zupljanin also mentioned to you when -- when he spoke about energy problems that were existent in the area, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He talked about the water being shut off for most at day -- maybe that was Radic -- the water being shut off for most of the day. Was there water when you were there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any problems with water any time you were there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly carried water in with us. I simply can't remember turning a tap on and seeing whether there was a flow or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you staying when you were in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we stayed overnight, we were in a hotel. I can't remember the name of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if that hotel had a generator or if it relied upon the power grid?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the hotel called the Golden Card?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could take you back to Banja Luka and show you the hotel. But at this time -- I simply can't remember what it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On page 8 of that first -- the report of that first meeting, there was some talk about a press release. And Mayor Radic asked you to change that press release to say that -- instead of being invited by Mr. Radic, you had been invited by the prime minister. And you told him that you could not do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he spoke of the prime minister, you understood, did you not, that he was speaking of the prime minister of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your conclusions, you determined that the top priorities of the people you spoke to were recognition - and when I say recognition, I mean recognition of Republika Srpska as an independent entity - and humanitarian aid for prisoners of wars, the refugees, and the population as a whole.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Humanitarian aid for their PWs. So the Serbs who were being held on the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, that probably would also include prisoners of war that were also being held that that area, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I think he was referring to the people in Rascani and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Exhibit 841.2 is a report of your second Banja Luka visit on 25 August 1992, just two days later. I assume you left Banja Luka and then returned.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned and went to meet with Mr. Radic again, he asked you immediately did you get permission from - and your report says - the Bosanska Krajinan government for your visit. You told us though in your testimony on Friday that he probably just said government and that you would have been the one that added "Bosanska Krajina" as kind of an assumption on your part. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if we go to my handwritten note, which would be quite tedious, we'll see the word "government" which was my shorthand for the Krajinan government. I think it was quite clear -- you can see a number of exchanges where this comes up, that what he's trying to do is to get us to recognise formally the government and we're having to dance around to make sure that we don't formally recognise the government, because we were not allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that government he was trying to get you to formally recognise was the Republika Srpska government.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at page 2 of the report -- it would be the third paragraph, beginning with the word: "It depends." The last sentence -- and this paragraph is talking about a next meeting. The last sentence says: "In the meantime, the HOM, which I understand means head of mission, and Djeric can provide the authorisation for your visits. None of us can make the decisions." Do you know who Djeric was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not certain on this point, but I think that he was the Serb representative in Geneva. I'm sure you could find somebody else who would recognise that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And on page 6 -- the bottom of page 5 and the top of page 6, Mr. Radic asked you if you could buy newspapers. He said that they have difficulties with papers. And it has something to do with different currencies and things. Could you explain that, tell me what that's about.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think that it was Barney who had asked Radic if we could buy newspapers, and Radic was then explaining that they were having difficulty getting hold of the paper with which to print the newspapers. I think that's -- that's what that conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But he talks about "You can't find a smaller area with more different currencies in use." There apparently was some question about which money was valid money at that point. Did you run across that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. And so again each of the parties either was or was alleging that the other was producing their own currency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The next report I want to visit with you about is your report of 1 September 1992 and your meeting with Ivastanin Nebojsa, the municipal president of Bosanska Gradiska. And that would be Exhibit 841.3, I believe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He identified their first problem as attacks [Realtime transcript read in error "a tax"] coming from Croatia, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you accept his report in that regard?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you could go back again to the UNPROFOR reporting at the time, which would give far more detail than I can remember. But I remember that there was an issue with the Croats going into UNPA North -- north? That would have been west. The UNPA just to the north of Gradiska anyway. I think it's UNPA West. And attacking -- or shelling from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can't remember the precise detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosanska Gradiska is located on the Sava River, which is the border between Croatia and Bosnia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far is -- is Gradiska from Banja Luka? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can show you on the map without seeing where the scale is on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you accept that it's about 50 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honours, there is a -- I believe it's a mistake. 24, 17 -- 18. The attacks coming from Croatia. It is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. As a tax.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is attacks and not a tax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are a hundred per cent right. You are a hundred per cent right. Definitely it was -- I heard the interpreters saying attacks coming from Croatia. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So counting on my map, I think it's 56 kilometres. It's got a route -- on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. The next thing that he spoke about after the attack from Croatia was a shortage of food, electricity, and water. And in that connection, he spoke of the blockade. Do you know what blockade he and other people were talk about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Fundamentally there was a blockade of Serbia and beyond that of all the Serb parts of both Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the effect of the blockade of Serbia on that part of Bosnia which could no longer get supplies from Croatia or Sarajevo was to also cut that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina off from any supply line.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. And again, I think there are references to it in here, to the fact that they had a very narrow corridor which they established at the very north --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: North-easten corner of Bosnia where they were able to get supplies through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But those supplies had to come from Serbia, which was subject to a blockade.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you do know that supplies from Croatia and Sarajevo had been cut off, of course, because of the war.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of normal commerce, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you look at paragraph 21, page 3 -- 21 and 22 actually. What Mr. Nebojsa told you was: "We wish to have our canton. We think that the principle of self-determination should be accepted." Do you know what he's talking about there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the ideas which was being floated by the parties and the International Community was that Bosnia should be divided into three cantons, which would be autonomous regions within the overall country of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is additional argument to some extent for the recognition of -- of Republika Srpska or some part thereof as a -- a Serb canton. And based on the international law principle of self-determination.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then he said to you, and you've reported this in paragraph 27: "So the best solution would be within the boundaries that each of these groups organise their lives as well as they can and then the process of integration happens in a natural way. In this way the wounds are healed." That's as close as you could recall to his actual words to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's me writing down what the interpreter was saying as they were interpreting what he was saying. So I, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he simply asked: "Help us in this, and you will make a great contribution to peace"; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the security situation you saw there in Bosanska Gradiska, and I think you said there were pickets every hundred metres or so which you thought was a significant security protection. In light of your knowledge that Gradiska was a border town, on the border between two warring parties, in the midst of a war, that probably wasn't an excessive amount of security, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstand. What they were doing was standing there lining the route, as you would do for a royal procession. So this was something on show for us, as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sort of treating you as semi-royalty.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly Sir John was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's go now to your third meeting with Mr. Radic, which would be your report at 841.4. And this was on the 1st of September, 1992. And on page 3 of that report -- and it's paragraph 17 -- it appears that he presented you with a fax which contained a plan for flights that would be carrying 560 tonnes of aid in seven days into Banja Luka, consisting of flour and medical supplies, controlled in Belgrade and by the International Community in Banja Luka. He told you that flight should have come in on the 26th -- the first of those flights should have landed on 26 June, in which the Red Cross would have received 14 tonnes of medicine and 9 tonnes of other medical supplies. And he says those flights were not allowed by the governments of Bosnia and Croatia because they did not open the air space from Belgrade to Banja Luka. Do you have any independent knowledge of that situation, beyond what Mr. Radic told you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. He told you about babies dying of lack of oxygen and people dying because there was no dialysis liquid fluids. Do you know anything about those situations beyond what you were told by Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a Mr. Popovic at that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you understood him to be a representative -- a Minister of Health or something from the government of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your reports here, you made three visits to Banja Luka. On how many of those visits did you actually remain overnight in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On those three visits, we stayed over once. And I think on subsequent visits, we'd stayed over again probably a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber what Banja Luka was like. I mean, what was it like being in Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a town that was very hot and dry in the summer, fairly quiet, not much vehicle movement, not surprisingly, because there was very little petrol. People moving around -- armed people moving around; not a town that had been damaged by any particular fighting that was obvious, but again that wasn't surprising because there hadn't been fighting there particularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it it didn't strike you as a town in the middle of a war.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that it was very quiet and there weren't a lot of vehicles moving around was actually a symptom of the fact that there was a war going on because of the blockade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The economic effect of that war?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you like. And the fact that there were a lot of people walking around carrying Kalashnikovs and wearing uniform, again perhaps a symptom of a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you see any roadblocks in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would hate to have to try to mark them on a map again. But certainly, there were roadblocks on the way in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. During the night that you were there, did you hear any shooting or any explosions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I can't -- I couldn't tell you which night and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what sort of things were going back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to speak with any of the non-Serb residents of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be consistent with what you saw to describe Banja Luka as a ghetto?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I would want to understand your definition of a ghetto. No. It was a town that was very quiet but not a -- not a ghetto.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go now to your report of 3 September, a short two-page report detailing your visit to Manjaca. We're told -- this is what your report says. And it's confused me. You were told that all Croat prisoners of war were to be exchanged on 1 September 1992. "I do not know if this actually happened." And it was actually the 3rd of September when you were there, two days after that. Is there a mistake there or what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Let's go back to the original and see what I've put in there. You even now have the copy that's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do. But I don't know where I'd find it, what page I'd find it on in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page -- it starts page 40, I think, Mr. Ackerman, and Mr. McLeod. If I'm not wrong, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't actually have a printed copy of that -- of those typed notes. If somebody has a spare, that would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could the usher hand him ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was the page, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the part of the notes starts on page 40, dealing with your visit to Manjaca --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- camp starts on page 40. But I can't find the reference that Mr. Ackerman has pointed -- or has asked you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's on page 49, "Tensions regarding PW." 6 -- number 6 on page 49. It says "Tuesday." Maybe you know in the context of the meeting what Tuesday was.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly wrote "Tuesday." If anybody has a diary which would take us back to that month of that year, we'll be able to work out what Tuesday was in terms of a date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're probably not going to get there, and I'm not sure it's that important, so let's just drop it. My guess is that you were referring to --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the following Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the following Tuesday, not the Tuesday before you got there. So that -- and that's probably a fair guess, is it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would make the same assumption as you have at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were also told that the -- the Muslim prisoners of war were available to be exchanged but the Muslims were not interested, they did not believe they were worth the effort. And then you said: "This is not true as demonstrated by events in the Middle East." What did you mean when you said that? It's paragraph 15 of that report, by the way.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember that at that time in the Middle East there were a series of either hijackings or hostage takings designed to get the Israelis to release Palestinian prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That -- that may or may not have had any relationship to what the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina believed with regard to exchange with the Muslims that were in that camp, however, and that doesn't necessarily indicate that wasn't true, does it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would then be a difference between what the Bosnian government wanted to do and just the laws of Islam. So I was making a comment about his interpretation, your point is correct, I think my point is also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. I agree with you. I now want to go to Exhibit 841.7, which is your 3 September meeting with Dr. Stakic in Prijedor. On page 3 you report that Dr. Stakic said this to you: "The main problem is that the Muslims wage their war with electricity. The result is that no one has electricity and CSCE can do something about it. It is much more important to have electricity than butter." Do you know what he meant by the statement "The Muslims wage war with electricity"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I think that he was referring to the fact that there were probably hydroelectric generating plants in Central Bosnia in areas controlled by the Muslims which would then have supplied power up to Northern Bosnia and that those transmission lines had been cut, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You visited Trnopolje, and yesterday you talked about the machine-guns you saw during that visit to Trnopolje. You were told they were there for the safety of the person staying there. And I think you expressed some scepticism about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know and did you know at the time, that there were roving bands of armed criminal extremists who were attacking places like Trnopolje and Manjaca for that matter? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told us that when we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know not about attacks on Manjaca by armed extremist groups, Serb extremist groups that were armed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody on either party had mentioned that to us on any occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you had known that, that, of course, would have changed your impression with regard to the contention that those machine-guns were there to protect the people that were there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that were the case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were asked by most people who spoke to you at Trnopolje that their primary question was when they were going to get out, when would they be able to leave there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they spoke about getting out and leaving there, they were speaking about getting out of the country.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And going somewhere else. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were, of course, free to walk away from the camp any time and go back to their homes, but they wanted to leave the country, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two things. Yes, they wanted to leave the country, and I think in practice they couldn't go back to their homes because their homes probably didn't exist any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. And you know that there was a reluctance on the part of the UN and UNHCR to assist people in leaving the country because of the fear that it would become -- they'd sort of become complicate in what at that time was known as ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you told us that it took a long time for UNHCR to process people to -- to leave the country because they'd have to interview each one and establish that they really wanted to leave before they would assist them in leaving.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the ICRC, who interviewed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: ICRC.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- each person individually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. I got it wrong in my notes. Okay. I want to go back to Manjaca for a few moments now. The people you saw as detainees in Manjaca, many of them were of military age, were they not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think one has to work out a definition for military age. And I think at that time in that place, anybody who was male over the age of about 14 was considered to be of military age, so yes, they were all of military age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was an Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a Muslim army, in operation, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that army along with the Croatian army was fighting against the Serbian army, the Army of Republika Srpska, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And young Serbian men were being killed by young Croatian and Bosniak men fighting in their separate armies during that fighting.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of those who were confined in Manjaca would have been perfect candidates and perfectly willing, I assume, to fight for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina given half a chance.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you know, don't you, of released prisoners who did exactly that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly met a man -- I wonder if this is what you're referring to -- in a Croatian prison in Central Bosnia the following year who had been in Manjaca and had been released and had then been picked up by the Croatian army. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The choices facing those responsible for keeping these people at Manjaca were to either keep them there, to send them to Bosnia-Herzegovina and face them on the front lines, or to send them to third countries basically.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a statement or a question, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a question. Those were the choices available: Keep them, send them to Bosnia-Herzegovina territory, or send them to third countries.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or allow them to stay at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think we just established that if they were allowed to stay at home, they would likely become part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and wind up in the front lines fighting against the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that if they had -- now, we're dancing on pinheads here. But I think if they had just stayed at home, they would have carried on being members of the population in that part of Bosnia, would otherwise have had to leave that part of Bosnia to get down eventually to join the Armija in Central Bosnia. If they had done that, then yes, they would have certainly joined the army, one can assume, or gone off to do some other job somewhere else in Europe, if they'd been able to. But there would certainly have been an option for them to have stayed at home and done whatever else it was they had been doing had it not been for the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know that Muslims from north-west Bosnia, the Krajina area of Bosnia, actually did leave there, become part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and fight against the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I met one person who had done that, so I can certainly say yes in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The United Nations and UNHCR were taking the position regarding all of these people, whether they were held in places like Manjaca or Trnopolje or any other place, that facilitating their departure from Bosnia-Herzegovina was something they were reluctant to do for fear of being complicate in ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fundamental position of the UN agencies was that people should be allowed to stay at home and live as part of that community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if they were rounded up and put in a camp and then told your option is to remain in this camp or leave, and the UN was going to facilitate that, then they would exactly be facilitating ethnic cleansing and all that would have to be done by whichever party wanted to carry out ethnic cleansing would be to round people up and put them into a camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder if you looking at that situation -- and I didn't plan to ask you this question, but I'm going to take the risk and just do it. I wonder if looking for that situation, you didn't start having the same kinds of feelings that caused you to leave the British army because of what was going on in Northern Ireland, that things were political rather than practical.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Northern Ireland, the army was trying to prosecute a counter-terrorist war which inevitably was not going to work because you had to deal with the terrorists through politics, which is what has now happened with some success. The issue in Bosnia was that at least two of the three parties felt that the solution was to remove those members of the community that didn't fit their ethnic mix, then solidify the borders of their canton, then hold elections and say "Look at us, we are democratic Europeans. We want to be part of Europe." But the process quite clearly was to get rid of the people that didn't fit first and then hold elections and be democratic. So yes, the problem was a political one, but I don't think that the practical solution was necessarily wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you spoke of your -- of your dismay upon seeing the conditions under which people, for instance, at Trnopolje were being forced to live. And there was an option that was not politically acceptable, and that was to let them go -- people who wanted to go, to let them go somewhere where they could have a more comfortable life until the war had been resolved, at least. Didn't that seem like the sensible thing to do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point - and if one goes back to what Mr. Stakic had said, when they had recently fought an election and the Muslims were actually the majority - therefore perhaps in the Prijedor area that was a majority population. You had the minority population using force to evict the majority population because they did not fit the pattern which the majority population -- of which the minority population, but you had control of the army and the weapons wanted to impose. To me that's not the right way of doing things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my wife says to me occasionally what do you want to do? Affix blame or solve the problem? And I agree with you that that might have been a way to affix blame, but there were people that were in stress, who were not getting enough to eat, who did not have sufficient shelter, and it seems to me -- and I'm just wondering if you'll agree with me -- that the solution to that was not to make them continue to endure that for political reasons.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one accept that is one has already taken steps which are very counter to the correct political way of running things, then yes, the answer is not to hold people in a concentration camp for any longer than you have to. At that point, I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had heard from everyone that you spoke to basically in Banja Luka, in Bosanska Gradiska, in Prijedor about the problems and the shortages of food and water that arose from the blockade and the economic situation that existed in Northern Bosnia at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- you told us that when you were at Manjaca you were able to speak to some of the prisoners in German but that guards would immediately come over and listen in to those conversations. You don't know if any of the guards understood German, do you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, because I didn't try to strike up a conversation in German with them to find out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You concluded from your visit that most, if not all, the persons detained in Manjaca were civilians.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told that they were not civilians, that they were military, that they had been captured wearing uniforms, that those uniforms had been confiscated for the use of the army and they were given civilian clothes to wear.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was told to you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us on Friday that that was very difficult to believe because the clothes they were wearing appeared to be their own clothes because they fit them properly.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us you were present then when everyone was finally released from Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said it was winter and that it was very cold.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that the detainees were standing outside in their normal clothes, those clothes that we just talked about.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that ICRC had provided them with some very nice new jackets, ski-type jackets, that they were wearing at that point in time? Let me help you. Dark blue, ski-style jackets with light blue, red, or yellow trim. Do you remember those jackets?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Now, there were people who were taking photographs, so I'm sure you could get a photograph which would prove it one way or the other way. But I can't remember jackets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think so. Didn't the ICRC also supply all of them with new shoes from the Banja Luka shoe factory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They were -- now, I think that my comment was that -- was made on the basis that there were certainly still people inside Manjaca who were not being released at that point and they were certainly still wearing just civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I'm -- I'm sorry that I can't remember the details that you're asking for, but there were certainly still people inside the buildings who were still just wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that inside Manjaca when you visited the inside of the camp that people were sitting on the floor for -- on their blankets for long periods of time. And I believe it was your conclusion that it must have been uncomfortable for them to -- to have had to sit on the floor for long periods of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they were sitting on the floor and that if they had been sitting on the floor for long periods of time, then it would have been excruciatingly painful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, whenever it's convenient, we'll break for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's convenient right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How much longer Mr. Ackerman thinks he's going to be roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then, of course -- are you -- is there going to be a cross-examination for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It will take about one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll break now and then we will have -- we'll continue after the break, resuming at five past 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were performing your duties for ECMM, you actually visited several different parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe it was your -- your habit or your usual behaviour that when you would go into a -- a new area that you were not familiar with, you would try to read as many reports as you could to familiarise yourself as much as possible with the area and what had been happening there before you got there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly the case in some places, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course that would certainly facilitate the efforts you were making if you had as much knowledge as you could possibly acquire about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you personally observed a great deal of what was going on in various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the times you were there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that what you saw was a conflict that was going on between citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina primarily divided along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats were fighting Serbs, and later Croats and Serbs were fighting Muslims.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you say that what you saw was by classic definition a civil war?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if a civil war is a war amongst the -- the members of a particular nation state, then yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You concluded at the end of all your visits that you talked about here to Banja Luka and the various camps that the Muslim population was being systematically kicked out of that area, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you told us was that this was common across all parts of the former Yugoslavia. One section of the community that was not wanted by another section of the community. So Muslims, Serbs, and Croats were all kicked out of certain areas by Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you will find -- and you're referring in part to things that I've said in previous Trial Chambers, I think -- that certainly Serbs were kicked out, Croats were kicked out, Muslims were kicked out, but the people who were doing most of the ethnic cleansing, if we want to use that term, were the Serbs and the Croats. And in my experience, the Muslims to a -- a far greater extent than the other two parties wanted to try and maintain some sort of ethnically mixed grouping. So I think there was far less evidence -- there was evidence, but I think there was far less evidence of the Muslims ethnically cleansing than the two other parties who most definitely did carry that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the presence in Banja Luka of -- of Serb refugees in fairly large numbers out of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there were a number of references to them, 176.000 refugees is the number which was mentioned a number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the pattern across the whole area, whether it in -- a Croat -- in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in those situations, it was nearly an identical pattern, wasn't it? Maybe I need to explain that. And if I do, you tell me.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be slightly more precise, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I will. You spoke about it in this way. You spoke about a -- a pattern of activity where women and children were separated from men, women and children were generally transported somewhere. Men were generally confined to somewhere and that that pattern repeated itself all across Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said -- and I think I would say now that the pattern particularly of separating women and children and removing them and putting the men into camps was something which we observed in Northern Bosnia, so I think that would be quite correct. It would also be quite correct to say that the basic principle of -- of ethnic cleansing was something which took place in most areas but that -- that precise methodology, if you like, is something which I'm comfortable saying that I witnessed and heard references to in Northern Bosnia but I wouldn't want to try and think of an example of exactly the same pattern somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you're not familiar with -- with the pattern, for instance, in the Konjic, area, Bradina area, in the southern part of the country, in the Celebici camp we -- I asked you about that earlier.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't -- I didn't go and talk to people down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Travnik? Are you aware of what happened in that area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail, not having been there myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I think that's all I have. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Yes. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to give up my position for Madam Fauveau and just sit over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. Thank you. Madam Fauveau will be cross-examining you, sir, on behalf of General Talic. Thank you. Cross-examined by Ms. Fauveau-Ivanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 you were working for the European mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start working for the European mission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you based in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the European mission worked in Bosnia and that it left Bosnia before the war. Do you know why the European mission left Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was considered by the member states of the ECMM that conditions within Bosnia as a whole were too dangerous. I think that a monitor had been killed fairly recently before that in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The observer who was killed, wasn't he killed near Mostar -- next to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain, but I think so.
