utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbian authorities in Banja Luka were opposed to the departure of European observers from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I wasn't there at the time, I don't know what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August 1992 you went to Banja Luka for the first time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go during that same period to other areas in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on did you go to other areas in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Central Bosnia in the Kiseljak-Zenica area - Christmas of that year - and back again the following May, and I was in Bihac on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The regions you went to, the areas you went to, were under the control of Muslims and Croats; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you visited these areas, you were able to observe the presence of Mujahedin there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there were people that were called Mujahedin in Zenica. I don't remember seeing anybody called Mujahedin in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before going to Banja Luka, you did inform the authorities in Banja Luka of your visit; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Banja Luka authorities immediately answered your request.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This answer was favourable.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were taking -- that you took notes at meetings. Did other members of your mission also take notes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that they did, but I don't have their notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When writing your reports, did you use their notes as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think you can see that my reports are to a large extent simply typing my handwritten notes, so they were almost entirely based on the notes that I took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other members of the mission, did they also write reports?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am fairly certain that Barney Mayhew would have written operational reports, but I don't have copies of most of the stuff that was written by ECMM, so I don't -- I certainly don't have copies of reports written by members of the team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that sometimes you'd be absent from the room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the parts of the conversation that took place during your absence aren't included in your reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at page 8 of your report of 25 August. It's P841.2. That is the exhibit number. It's the second meeting with the Mayor Radic. That's what it is about. At the bottom of that page, you wrote: [In English] The Serbs hold 64 per cent of area. Mr. Karadzic estimated in his statement to CNN that Serbs will not retain more than 50 per cent." [Interpretation] Is this paragraph something that Mr. Radic said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time of this position of Karadzic's, to keep 50 per cent of the territory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember at this stage the exact positions of the negotiations at that point at the -- or building up to the London conference. I'm sure there are other people who were actually involved in the negotiations who would give a far better answer than I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serb proposition for the Lisbon conference was to have 46 to 49 per cent of the territory? That is what the Serbs had suggested.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I wasn't a party to those negotiations, so I -- and I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, this position that Radic expressed concerning 50 per cent, that corresponds more or less to the Dayton agreement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I don't have a copy of Dayton, so I can't confirm that, but I would assume that it's probably correct if you think that it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that the Serbs obtained 49 per cent of territory in accordance with the Dayton agreement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't have a copy of the Dayton agreement, and I don't remember the precise details of percentages. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless this percentage had been put forward when you were in Banja Luka according to your report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The percentage that I reported was the number which Radic mentioned during the meeting. I simply don't have the details which would show how that percentage had been arrived at through the negotiations and where it ended up towards Dayton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At meetings with the Mayor Radic, you spoke about freedom of movement and he told you that you could have freedom of movement but not in the entire area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the zones, the areas under Muslim or Croat control, you didn't have total freedom of movement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be fair to say that as a principle, ECMM didn't have full freedom of movement in the other areas. To give a precise answer, I'm not sure that we tested that -- that I personally tested that theory in each of the other areas. But as a principle, there were certainly areas controlled by each of the parties where ECMM was not able to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was common in war zones not to be able to go everywhere; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But again, the principle under which the ECMM was trying to operate was that it had full access to all areas and particularly, for example, in Croatia where it was established to try and monitor the -- the cease-fire it had to have access to the contact line to see that there were not heavy weapons which had been brought up to the contact line. So the theory was access anywhere. The practice was that there would be areas where it would be difficult to go to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the European mission itself was also preoccupied with the security of its members. It was concerned about their security.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be correct to say that in 1992 in Bosnia there were snipers everywhere; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not everywhere, but certainly along the contact lines it would not be uncommon to find snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would be correct to say that there were also minefields.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, along contact lines, certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you visited Banja Luka, you were escorted by the police; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were escorted -- I simply can't remember whether it was a police vehicle or a military vehicle, but almost certainly police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member of the British army, and you're not sure whether it was a police vehicle or a military vehicle; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that ten years later I can't remember whether it was a military vehicle or a police vehicle, but certainly we were escorted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at your report regarding the meeting with the mayor of Bosanska Gradiska. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit P841.3. It's page 3. It's the last paragraph, and it's item 26. In this paragraph, the jihad is referred to. Was it the mayor of Bosanska Gradiska who referred to the jihad?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as you said, you did meet Mujahedin in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that I was aware that there were people that were called Mujahedin in Zenica. To take that a step further, it was a -- it was a matter of very great interest to the International Community whether there were Mujahedin and a lot of people were trying to find Mujahedin and they had very little success. So I did not personally see people that I think were Mujahedin, but I know that in Zenica there were people who people referred to as Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Colonel Popovic, whom you -- who visited -- when you visited Manjaca, he spoke to you about the Geneva Conventions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Colonel Popovic was fully aware of the Geneva Conventions. He had knowledge of these conventions.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Colonel Popovic spoke to you about the embargo which had been imposed on Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to check my notes? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you or someone else remarked that the embargo was not applicable -- didn't concern medical supplies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would have been Sir John Thomson who made that comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wouldn't be true to say that all the transactions - and that included medicine and food - all these transactions were subject to control?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: What control do you mean? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The control of the competent authorities, so they could check that medicine and food was actually -- were actually the items in question.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that if there had been humanitarian aid which was being taken in, then it would have been subject to control, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a country under sanctions always has more difficulties in procuring medications and food than a country which is not subject to sanctions.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I am competent to say that a country under sanctions would always have particular difficulties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be correct to say that the embargo imposed on Yugoslavia had consequences for the entire economy of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, the population -- the entire population of a country under sanctions feels the consequences of the embargo.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these consequences are felt primarily in the form of lack of certain products, shortages.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the embargo was imposed on Yugoslavia on the 30th of May, 1992 by virtue of the resolution number 757?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. By the time you got to the end of the translation, I couldn't see what the point was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the embargo was imposed on Yugoslavia on the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not precisely, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm hesitant to interrupt but it does seem to me we're drifting well away from this witness's area of competence. This is all general history and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he is but nonetheless, Your Honour, I don't think this is particularly relevant to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Ms. Korner. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that this embargo lasted until after the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And again I'm probably not the right person. But I'm sure you could simply get hold of the relevant UN resolution which would tell you what the answer was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Banja Luka, in that period, Banja Luka was able to procure products only from Yugoslavia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in practice, there was a very thriving black market and a great deal of things were being brought across the Sava River. But again, that is what I believe was happening, as opposed to what I actually saw myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say from the other side of the Sava River, are you talking about the territory of Croatia under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that things would have gone from Croatia under Croatian control into Croatia under Serbian control into Northern Bosnia under Serbian control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, it's what I believe was happening, but I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any rate, officially the products available in the area of Banja Luka originated from Yugoslavia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said that you had in mind there was a very thin corridor linking Banja Luka with Yugoslavia -- linking Bosanska Krajina with Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that this corridor was opened not long after your arrival in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when it was opened, but I was certainly very familiar with the fact that people were travelling backwards and forwards using that corridor. So it was a fact of life for most of the time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August 1992 you visited the camp of Manjaca. Did you visit in 1992 any camps under Muslim or Croat control?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- well, in 1992 -- I think it was 1992 we went into Bihac to take Serb detainees from Bihac all the way back round to Belgrade. At the time that we picked them up, I don't know whether we were collecting them from the camp that they had been held in or just a place where the ICRC had been told to -- to collect the detainees. It was some sort of factory building, so I don't know whether it was a prison or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing any Croat or Muslim-run camp in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know whether the place where we picked up the Serb prisoners was a camp. It didn't look like a camp. And then I didn't see a Croat camp in Bosnia until 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as Manjaca is concerned, you said that the prisoners did not wear uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since they were not in uniform, you concluded that they were not prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a combination of the fact that they were not wearing uniforms and the fact that they said that they were civilians led me to believe that they were not prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be fair to say that in former Yugoslavia a lot of people carried weapons?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those armed people often organised themselves into groups; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be the other way around, that there were people who were in groups who were then armed as opposed to people suddenly finding they had weapons in their hands and forming groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all those armed people in groups, not all of them wore uniforms, did they?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that almost all of the people that I saw on each side who were carrying weapons were wearing a uniform of some sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never saw in Bosnia or in Croatia people in civilian clothes who still had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly saw people wearing civilian clothes who were bodyguards for various dignitaries and they were wearing civil clothes. But I think I -- the vast majority of the people that I saw carrying, for example, a Kalashnikov were wearing uniform. The gentleman from Pale were wearing civilian clothes, and he had a pistol in his belt and he was carrying a very nice German machine pistol in his car. So certainly there were exceptions. But majority of people would be wearing uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go for the first time to Bosnia in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the first time I'd actually been inside Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that at the very beginning of the war in Bosnia, in April, a lot of people carried weapons but did not wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about a certain Canadian, Glasnovic. Do you remember that man?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the CSC rapporteur mission was a Canadian, and I think he had been asked to try and find a Canadian, and so this is the person that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct to say that this Davor Glasnovic was a Canadian mercenary who was hired by the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you couldn't see everything when you were in Manjaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the part that you were not able to see was in fact outside the camp, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on your definition of the camp. It was outside the wire which contained the cattle sheds but certainly within the -- within the environs of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This area that you were not able to see was outside of the part where the prisoners were held; is that true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was outside the area where the cattle sheds where the men were kept for the majority of the time but we know that the prisoners were taken out of the cattle sheds to go to work, and therefore it was certainly within the area where it was possible for the prisoners to be. I can't remember now exactly what it was that prompted us to go and look at these facilities, but at the time there must have been something that prompted us to say, "Can we go and look here?" Which prompted the response, "No, you can't."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that Manjaca was a military compound?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was evident as we arrived up the road from Banja Luka that we were entering a military training area or what looked to me as an ex-soldier like an military training area. There was a military camp on the road. And then we turned right and drove along the side of a very shallow valley. And on the left-hand side as we were driving along the valley was then what was obviously a farm which had been converted into a camp -- into a Detention Centre, concentration camp, call it what you will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any rate, this part that you were not able to see could have been a training area, a military training zone.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- now, at this stage I can't remember exactly what it was, but it was certainly within what was definitely originally a farm, which was distinct from the military camp back on the main road. So there may well have been a military reason why they didn't want us to see something, or it may well have been -- or it may possibly have been that there were people there or things there that didn't want us to see. But this was certainly within Manjaca, the detention centre, which as I've described earlier on was formerly a farm and it was within the farm compound that we were asking to go. We didn't want to go see back on the main road anything to do with the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any rate, you allow the possibility that you were not able to see -- that you were not allowed to see that area for military reasons.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we were being told by the commandant that we were free to see anything, and we said can we go and see something, and the question was ignored, which meant that we were not able to go and see something. That's all I can report now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Serbian Minister for Health said that he was ready to sign an order for the closing of all camps on behalf of the Serbian government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I said -- I have noted that he was from the health ministry. I think your colleague gave him the title the Minister of Health. I wasn't sure about that. And I believe he said that yes, he was in a position to sign a paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact several months later such an order was signed by Radovan Karadzic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And indeed consequently the ICRC went in and started to take people out of the camps, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When that order was signed by Radovan Karadzic, it was concluded, it was decided that prisoners of all three parties be freed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact the Croats and the Muslims did not keep their promise. Serb prisoners were not freed. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that that is not correct because I certainly personally saw Serb prisoners being released by the Muslims from Bihac and I drove a very long journey with them back to Belgrade, and colleagues of mine from the ECMM accompanied the ICRC in other parts of Bosnia where other prisoners of other groups were being released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not saying that they -- there were no Serb prisoners who were released, but the agreement was all prisoners -- for all prisoners, according to my information, not all Serb prisoners were released.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the details, but I think that in practice all three parties hung onto a number of prisoners for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report concerning the Manjaca camp, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 841.6. And that's page 2, paragraph 15. You wrote: [In English] "We were told that the Muslim war prisoners were available for exchange but that there was no interest in this from the Muslim side. The explanation was given that the Muslims do not believe that prisoners are worthy of effort. This is not true, as events in the Middle East demonstrate." [Interpretation] You concluded it was not true in the light of what happened in the Middle East. Are you familiar with the Middle East?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that time one of the other stories that was playing on Sky News and CNN was the fact that the -- one of the many Palestinian organisations was either carrying out hijackings or holding hostages -- I can't remember exactly which -- in order to facilitate the release of Palestinian detainees being held by the Israelis. And at the time that was a very current issue and that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But please tell us, in the Middle East was it about prisoners of war or simply prisoners?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it depends on your point of view. It would be fair to say that these were Arabs or Palestinians who were being detained by the Israelis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't translated. Sorry, I got French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any rate all your knowledge about the developments in the Middle East are based on what you saw in television; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak at the time about this problem to anyone from the Muslim government, about the fact that there were Muslim prisoners available for release or for exchange but there is no goodwill to proceed with that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was a debate which was being conducted in a different -- at a different level to the level that I was operating at by different people. So certainly that conversation was taking place, but I was not a party to that conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally didn't know what the position of the Muslim government was with regard to the Muslim prisoners at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten years later on I wouldn't want to try and hazard a precise response to that. At the time I probably knew pretty much exactly what the position was, but now I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said last Friday, the 21st of June, that you had been to another camp while you were in the British army. In which country was this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in England.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were the prisoners in that camp?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: British soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't really a prisoner of war camp, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I think I was saying that I had been inside a prison which was a military prison. I think the point that was being made, that I had experience of military prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the United Kingdom is on a totally different level economically compared to the former Yugoslavia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it wasn't in a state of war, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on your point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no war on the territory of England, Wales, or Ireland.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would certainly depend on your point of view. If you talked to the current education minister in Northern Ireland, he was definitely feeling like a combatant in the war against the British at that point in Northern Ireland and on the mainland territory of the UK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also spoke about the antipathy, hostility between the Scots and the English.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Scotsmen and English fought on the same side in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let her finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm just a bit concerned as to how long this is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I think we are nearing the end. This is what I remember right now, that your very first question was "What's your name? Is it correct that you're Charles McLeod?" And he said not exactly, it's Charles George Alexander or whatever. So more or less it explains the Scottish-English balance of powers, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that I actually said that the Scots and the English fought on the same side in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. That was my question. I asked you if Scottsmen and the English fought on the same size shoulder to shoulder in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that during the Second World War Serbs fought on one side and the Muslims and Croats on the other? I don't think that all of my question was interpreted. I said Muslims and Croats fought on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact the translation that I have on the transcript is: "Do you know that during the Second World War Serbs fought on one side and Muslims on the other?" The question actually included also the Croats, together with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I knew that the -- to an extent you had Croats on one side and Serbs on another side, I didn't actually know which side the Muslims were aligned with.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that Croats actually fought on the side of fascist Germany.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Paddy Ashdown visited the Manjaca camp in 1992 in August?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were present during the release of prisoners from Manjaca in November 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was the 14th November 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have my diary now, but it was -- if that's the date that I have said before when I had my diary in front of me, then I'll accept that that was the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was -- it's the date which features in your witness statement given to the OTP on the 16th of March, year 2000, page 4.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So on that occasion I had my diary with me and that was the date in the diary, so yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were released on that day?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly at this moment, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on that occasion one person made a speech thanking the camp authorities at Manjaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this speech was held in your presence and in the presence of the Red Cross; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this person who made the speech, this prisoner, was released on that same day from Manjaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that individual was then released, but I would assume since he was standing on the outside with the group who were released that he probably was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that person was liberated, he would have left in the direction of Croatia together with the Red Cross, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact that person would have had no other reason to make that speech unless he really meant it.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that person was probably told to make that speech very publicly under duress as opposed to saying what he really thought. That's my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when this person gave the speech, the Red Cross was already present; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a slightly naive view to think that somebody would not say something under duress simply because they were standing and about to leave is my view.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness the photograph which is Exhibit 842.2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This photograph was taken in August 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that point in time there was no fighting in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally didn't observe, didn't see the destruction of these two houses that we can see in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know how these two houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the two houses which were destroyed and which we can see, that they belonged to Muslims and that the house which is intact belonged to a Serb. Could you tell me the identity of those who owned the houses that had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm making a comment based on my experience of seeing a similar pattern right across the former Yugoslavia, where you would find houses in a village which had been destroyed and other houses which had not been destroyed. And I'm saying in light of that experience, I would infer that these are houses which are occupied, on the one hand, Muslims, who are no longer there, and on the other hand, by a Serb who looks as if he is still living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know who the owner of the house which is intact is either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact this is an assumption of yours.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that that was clear from what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Korner, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is. Re-examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. McLeod, you were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That in relation to the camps, one of the reasons for these camps, in particular Manjaca, as I understand it, was to keep out marauding bands of Serbs. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you, please, to have a look at a document which is exhibited as Prosecutor's Exhibit -- that's a good point. My volume didn't have it. It's in the volume 4 of the Banja Luka documents, and it's dated the 27th of July, 1992. And it's got the disclosure number 4.674 and I'm sorry, because I had a volume without the numbers on them, I'm just going to check?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's apparently something wrong with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. With the question. The transcript indicates was asked by Ms. Korner. I don't think that's the question she asked. Starting 19, 20, and 21 I don't think that's -- just look, Ms. Korner. I don't think that's your question, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Ackerman, it was your suggestion that that's how the question came out, that these camps had been established because there were bands of Serbs marauding around the place. Are you saying that wasn't your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I certainly asked no such question, Your Honours. My -- my question had primarily to do with the machine-guns that he saw at Trnopolje that he was told were there to protect the people that were there and that he didn't believe that, and we had had testimony from one of the people from Manjaca that there had been an attack by some -- attack on Manjaca by some armed Chetniks, and I was just asking him if he knew about that. I never suggested the camps were designed to protect people from roving bands of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately at the moment we have a monitor that we can't seem to get today's LiveNote on, so I want to go back to see the exact question that Mr. Ackerman asked. But if there's no suggestion, then I don't need to trouble the witness with this document, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My impression is that there was such a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that was mine as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not exactly the way you have phrased it now, Mr. Ackerman, but more or less this was common practice that one had to be cautious because there was always this constant threat of these groups, possibly assailing one of these camps. Although you did not phrase it the way you phrased it a minute ago. I mean, but that's the impression they got, anyway. But if it's -- if I got you wrong, then -- then you are obviously right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Well, we obviously both got the same impression, Your Honour, I think certainly the way the question -- Mr. Ackerman didn't phrase it that way as he's just phrased it now. If there's no suggestion at all that these camps -- or these gun emplacements had nothing to do with the Serbs trying to attack the inmates, though I'm not going to bother --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that was certainly my position with regard to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what was Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Manjaca was only being used as an example of a situation where we have testimony that some band of Chetniks tried to attack the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not that it was there for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to put this document in any event, if I can just find the P number. I think it's P399. If that could be handed to the witness and we'll put it on the ELMO so -- because I don't imagine Your Honours have got the Banja Luka 4 volume with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I think we actually looked at it before. We did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We did. I don't remember when and in relation to which witness, but we certainly did look at this before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's dated the 27th of July, 1992. Stepping up security measures in defence of the prisoner of war camp order. "On the basis of the demonstrated need to step up security measures in the Manjaca prisoner of war camp because of possible interventions and actions aimed at forceful liberation of the prisoners from the outside or from within, and with a view to organising and taking measures to step up the security and the defence of the camp and prevent actions aimed at liberating the prisoners, I hereby issue the following." And there's a long list of -- which I needn't trouble you with, Mr. McLeod, of the security measures. With your military background, if there had been a perceived risk by the command of the 1st Krajina Corps that there were going to be attacks on the prisoners from outside, would you have expected that to be something that was mentioned and -- well, first of all, would you have expected something like that to have been mentioned?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on the timing of the various attacks. But looking at this, it's quite clear that what they're referring to is the need to increase security, to prevent removal of prisoners as opposed to people trying to get their hands on the prisoners to do damage to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then could we move to another document, please. This is in relation to these suggestions or rather the comment that what else could the Serbs be expected to do but lock up or deport people who might fight against them. Could you have a look now, please, at another document which is in the same Banja Luka volume 4. It's P408.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, this is a document, Your Honour, we've looked at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the 1st Krajina Corps command, dated the 6th of August, department for intelligence and security affairs. A selection of prisoners in the Manjaca POW camp. "By processing the war prisoners in the Manjaca POW camp we realised that a certain (quite large) number of them, according to incrimination, do not deserve to be treated as prisoners of war (they did not have weapons, they did not participate in combat, they were not in uniform, et cetera). "In order to free space to accommodate potential new prisoners in the Manjaca POW camp and in order for each prisoner to get the treatment they deserve, we ask that you send a responsible official (or several of them) to the camp, who would together with the Security Organ (at Manjaca) carry out a selection of persons who could be released and persons who must remain in the camp. This is all in aid of the proposal and the release of that section of the prisoners who do not fall into the prisoner of war category. "According to our records, in Manjaca there are currently 944 prisoners from the Sanski Most municipality. "As you know, we have recently been attacked by the European and world media in connection with the existence of "concentration camps." So this is a sufficient reason to carry out prisoner selection." Now, first, Mr. McLeod, what do you say about this and the suggestion or the comment that was made that the Serbs could do nothing but lock up people who could carry a weapon effectively?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's fascinating to see that piece of paper. It's quite clear looking at that that they knew that a large number of the people that they were holding in Manjaca were civilians who shouldn't have been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this comes from the chief of the Security Organ of the -- it's stamped 5th, but it was then the 1st Krajina Corps, a Colonel Bogojevic. With your military experience, Mr. McLeod, if the chief of security within a corps you would discovered that people were being held improperly, to put it at its lowest. Would that be a matter of concern to the security officer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would depend. I think under the circumstances he is likely to be the person who is working out whether it's a good idea or not to be seen to be holding these people opposed to whether or not it is a good idea to be holding them. Certainly if one takes the Geneva Conventions, then it's a command responsibility to be carrying out the Geneva -- to be implementing the Geneva Conventions, and as such if he's part of the chain of command responsible for managing the camps, then he absolutely has a responsibility to make sure that there are not people in there. But looking at that letter, that doesn't seem to be his concern. He's simply trying to create some space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a matter that within a corps command should have been brought to the attention of the person in command of the corps?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had thought that all the people that they were holding were soldiers and suddenly they realised that a large proportion of them were not soldiers - although I find it hard to believe that they could have found themselves in such a situation in the first place - but if they suddenly realised that they had a whole load of people who should not have been held there, then that would absolutely have been a command responsibility to fix in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally just one last document on this topic. Could you be shown please Prosecutor's Exhibit 415.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could just put that on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Because otherwise we won't be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's headed "Manjaca, 20th of August, 1992. "Meeting regarding the position on the treatment and prominence of persons who participated in armed disturbances." Present: Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, Major Stupar, coordinator of Security Organs of the Krajina Corps, and inspector and somebody unidentified. And then finally -- I'm leaving out introductory remarks. "A list of 92 individuals for whom there's no evidence of executing/participating in military activities. They are quite ill and their appearance is attracting attention from the media and humanitarian organisations." And then there's effectively a list of all these people. Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have any questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We don't have any questions, which means that your testimony comes to an end here. On behalf of the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for having come over to give your evidence. You will now be escorted out of the courtroom and given all the attention you require, either to return immediately to where you would like to return or I understand that he's still -- he's still -- his presence is still required here or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. McLeod is required in -- in the Stakic case tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the Stakic case. Yes. So you will be required to give evidence in another case. As far as this case is concerned, you're free to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll break for another 15 minutes or so and we will start with the new witness 7.112.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley is going to be calling the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, we don't have any protective measures in place. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's right, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Islamcevic, could I ask you to stand up, please. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you know, you've come here to give evidence. And according to our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, you are first required to make a solemn declaration that you will tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the declaration is contained on the piece of paper that you have just been handed. And you will be asked to read that aloud, please. That will be your solemn undertaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Willingly, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. So let me -- before the Prosecution starts putting questions to you, let me explain to you a little bit where you are and what's going to happen. If you look at my direction, I'm the Presiding Judge, and I am flanked on either side by two other Judges. Together we form this Trial Chamber which is hearing this case and which will ultimately decide it. My name is Agius and I come from the island of Malta; to my right is Judge Janu from the Czech Republic, and to my left is Judge Taya from Japan. Right in front of us is the member from -- is the team for the Registry. They will be monitoring the proceedings as we go along and assisting the Chamber. And to your right in the front row is the team for the Prosecution. The gentleman in the middle wearing the robe is Mr. Cayley and he will be the one to conduct the examination -- the so-called examination-in-chief, which will start today and which presumably will continue tomorrow. I do not anticipate that you will be in a position to conclude today, Mr. Cayley? No. Then tomorrow after Mr. Cayley finishes with his direct examination of you for the Prosecution, you will be examined by the two Defence teams. And the two Defence teams are in the front row on your left. The first three persons represent the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin, and the last two persons represent the Defence for General Talic. Having said that, you will now be asked a set of questions by the officer for -- appearing for the Prosecution, Mr. Andrew Cayley. Mr. Cayley, the witness is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, your name is Besim Islamcevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Besim Islamcevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were born in Sanski Most in 1955; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are by nationality a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are of Islamic faith; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your presence in Sanski Most, am I right in saying that apart from go periods of absence for your national service and for employment reasons you've lived all of your life in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 757.2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, whereabouts in Sanski Most did you live in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the Podbrijezje local commune, number 74 through 2 in the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the map next to you on the overhead projector -- you'll have to look at it next to you. Could you point to the Judges the village or commune of Podbrijezje.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness points at the village which is indeed shown on the map with the word -- with the name "Podbrijezje."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that your commune was on the road to Prijedor, on the main road to the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the N15 main road from Sanski Most to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to direct your mind to March and April of 1992. And I think I'm right in saying that at that time you were working at the Zdena pump station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: On the pump station to provide the town of Sanski Most and the surroundings with drinking water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in is events that you observed from your workplace at the pump station. Did you ever see military trucks in and around the Zdena area when you were working at the pump station?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: I think it would be best to clarify certain things, first of all, to clarify the fact that this is a working place and it required a working system consisting of four shifts: The first shift for two days, the second for two days, this third for two days, and the fourth -- two days would be -- the next two days would be free. During that period in the morning and in the afternoon and in the evening I was present in the working place in the local commune called Zdena, or rather in the immediate vicinity of the social centre. What you have said is correct. Towards the end of March and at the beginning of April while going to the nearby shop to get food for dinner I saw in the street where the shop was located, which was part of the social centre, which had offices on the -- on the floor, about 100 metres further down below I saw two lorries, olive-drab colour, and I noticed people too wearing olive-drab colour uniforms. That surprised me, and I noticed people moving and I noticed that something was being unloaded from the lorries and I could make out that they were unloading rifles. I didn't stay there for long because I was afraid to do so. I was afraid that as a witness I might have to suffer the consequences. I returned to my workplace. That was at dusk. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any conclusion at the time as to who was unloading rifles?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: A lot of things were clear to me during the days before and afterward in the social centre in Zdena a group of people met, people who belonged to the Serbian Democratic Party. I had the opportunity to observe that, and Mr. Vrkes Vladimir, president of the Serbian Democratic Party in Sanski Most was present, the president of the Sanski Most municipality was present, Mr. Nedeljko Rasula --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I want to keep your evidence quite focussed. We'll get on to this, but I'm asking you specifically about the events with the truck. You observed weapons being unloaded from the truck. Who was unloading the weapons from the truck?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: People wearing olive-drab uniforms. The lorry belonged to the JNA; that's logical. And people of Serbian nationality were there who were wearing military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was receiving the weapons that were being unloaded, if you know the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: In each case, it was the inhabitants, the inhabitants who were there and who lived around the social centre in the streets Kolonija 1, Kolonija 2, Kolonija 3. And a hundred per cent or at least 95 per cent of the population is Serbian there. So these were people of Serbian nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, also focussing on this time period March and April of 1992. Had you heard of an organisation called SOS or Serbian defence forces, SOS?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had, and I personally saw certain members of that formation in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you understand these people to be, the members of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? What were these people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their function? What was their role within the community in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know they were the first who started shooting in Sanski Most -- or rather, disturbing law and order, shooting from weapons, from zoljas, hand-held rocket launchers, and they would also blow up certain shops, certain establishments. And this information is information I obtained in the town from people who were more familiar with this matter. And if you allow me to say this, they didn't really make an effort -- much of an effort to conceal this. They walked around, and their insignia were quite clear. There was the SOS inscription which they had on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that they blew up certain shops, certain establishments. Shops and establishments belonging to whom in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to this whole line because he says, "This is information I obtained in the town from people who were more familiar with this matter." In other words, he has no person knowledge of this at all. If he can identify those people and was he talked to them and that kind of thing, then I would remove my objection. But I think this is not -- he's not testifying from his own knowledge at all at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I response to that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He also said that nobody made any kind of effort to conceal what was going on. I mean, in effect that this was public knowledge. It wasn't a secret as to what the SOS were doing in Sanski Most. And I'll ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the best way to go about it. Put a direct question, and -- because otherwise, I mean, it's not something which is unusual in these proceedings, Mr. Ackerman. I mean, the way he's going about it and the way the question was put and the way the question was answered is not in any way unusual. I mean, I do understand your point and I take your point, but I think there's an easy -- easy remedy for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, here's the thing I'm starting to worry about: It would very well be that what he heard he heard from someone else in town he heard last week in preparation for testifying here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, I think that the Prosecutor must set more of a foundation than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ackerman, I take your point, and I think Mr. Cayley knows how to deal with it. Please, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the target? You've said that shops and establishments were blown up. Who did those shops and establishments belong to in Sanski Most? That's the first question, before you deal with anything to do with what the gentleman on the Defence bench has said. So if you can answer that question first, what I'm putting to you, and I'll come on to the other point in a moment.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: In each case they belonged to Bosniaks; that is to say, Muslims, without exception. And I heard these explosives. Each explosion made my house shake. It's 1.200 metres as the crow flies. The town and the house that I lived in. Obviously I couldn't see all this but I heard all these explosions. And in the morning, in the course of the day, I obtained this additional information. I apologise. This wasn't a few days ago. I lived through all this. I experienced all this personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying that you did not see anybody physically plant explosives in any of these buildings, did you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: You're right in saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that the SOS were the people that were engaged in blowing up these buildings?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Certain members of the SOS would brag about it. The late Dusko aka Njonja, his deputy Mudrinic Dusko. They -- that was no secret at the time. Vojo Drazenovic, known as Vojvoda. They didn't hide this. This was success for them. It was a well-known fact in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally hear them bragging, these individuals that you've named? Did you hear them bragging about the fact that they'd been planting bombs in Muslim establishments in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that I didn't hear this from them -- I didn't hear them saying this directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear it from that they'd been bragging about blowing up Muslim establishments in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: People I knew. From acquaintances, friends in the town, both from Muslims and from some Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name any of those people? If you can remember. I know it's ten years ago. If you can remember any of the people that gave you this information.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: In each case -- for each case I can remember certain names, some of the names. But the person I heard this from, Mr. Rajlic Slavko -- Slavko Rajlic, a doctor from Sanski Most, respected citizen of Sanski Most who was also a Serb but a good man. I heard this from him. He was one of the persons I heard this from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to now direct your mind to the 25th of May of 1992. And I think I'm right in saying that this was your last working day at the marketplace in Sanski Most. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think after that time you had to return the keys for the marketplace and for the funeral parlour. You had to return your official keys. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm also right in saying that around this time there was a call for the Muslim members of the community to hand in any weapons that were in their possession. Do you recall that demand?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: I have to answer the first part of your question first. On the 25th of May, at about 11.20, half past 11.00, a colleague from work wrote to me and he said - Vojin Milorad - "Don't you see anything happening? Can't you see --" I said no. "Can't you see that something isn't okay in the town and that something is happening? It would be good for you to go and hand something in.." I did this. Then there was an announcement. They asked for weapons to be surrendered, not just in the Podbrijezje local commune but in the entire municipality under local Sanski Most radio, broadcast this and repeated this information on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you handed something in. What did you hand in to the authorities?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: There's no translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. First the daily -- the cash that I had at the market and then the keys that I had at the marketplace, and the additional equipment that I had also been issued with, that me and my colleague had been issued with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hand in a pistol that belonged to you, to the Serb authorities in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the local commune of Podbrijezje on a certain date all the -- there was a certain day when all the citizens of that local commune had to go to the social centre and they had to surrender weapons. I and the other inhabitants surrendered weapons. I can say that these weapons were ones which we owned legally, had permits, mostly for pistols and hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for the next 15 to 20 days I don't think you moved around the municipality of Sanski Most very much, did you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. There was not much movement. I went out on two or three days, and I tried not to get involved in anything and not to talk much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there came a time after this 20-day period when Teufik Hasic came to see you. Do you recall that time?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what Mr. Hasic came to see you about.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I should clarify one thing to the Chamber. Teufik Hasic is a local from the Podbrijezje commune. He was on good terms with the father of Vlado Vrkes because they worked together in the Sanu company [phoen], so he had the opportunity of talking to the father of Vlado Vrkes and finding out what the position of the Serbs was in Podbrijezje, and he learnt and told the rest of us that this gentleman had told him that Podbrijezje was also planned for evacuation. It was the northern gate of Sanski Most and therefore important for the Serbian authorities, and as such it would be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of questions for you. Mr. Hasic was a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Teufik Hasic is a Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this time who did you understand Vlado Vrkes to be?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Would you care to clarify. In which sense?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What function did Vlado Vrkes have in the municipality of Sanski Most, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, now I understand. I just have to say one thing before that. I knew Mr. Vlado Vrkes from before as a member of the League of Communists committee. He was very well read, well educated. He had returned from his university studies very recently. And first Mr. Rasula was appointed president of the SDS, and then Vrkes took over from him. So he became president of the SDS party in Sanski Most. To your question, I can say that at that time he was a man who was able to help or to refuse to help. On his position of the president of the SDS party he was as powerful, if not more powerful, than the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that you were told by Mr. Hasic that it was planned that the commune of Podbrijezje was to be evacuated. By evacuation, what do you mean? And who was to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I say "evacuated," I mean that people had to depart from the homes they occupied for centuries and that was forced movement, forced evacuation, primarily of women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who? Which people in your commune were to be, as you state, forcibly moved?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly Bosniaks, Muslims. Certainly not the Serbs from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as far as you can recall, can you explain to the Judges the process that a citizen had to go through in order to leave the municipality of Sanski Most, the administrative procedure that they had to go through in order to depart.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: I can say with complete certainty that in addition to the announcement that people wanted to leave voluntarily, quote unquote, you also had to produce certain papers, such as certificates that you paid your duties to the municipality, such as your electricity, your telephone bills, public utility bills, rent, and also a statement from your bank that you have no outstanding dues. When you gathered and prepared all these documents, you submitted them to the municipal authorities and filled in a form with your personal details. And in that form, there was also a line to the effect that each one of us was signing that document voluntarily and signing away our property to the Serb authorities; that is, to the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you a question which you may think is somewhat foolish. But we have to look at this transcript in months to come and I want to make it absolutely clear. Why do you say people who wanted to leave voluntarily, quote unquote? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Obviously there is a meaning implied. Who in their right mind would leave their home of their own free will together with all their property and the land they had lived on for many years? The Serb authorities did not want or could not provide guarantees of our personal security, could not guarantee that people would receive pensions, that their children would be able to continue going to school as before, could provide no guarantee of anything. To put it simply, there was no place for Muslims in Sanski Most any more in the new concept of life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that Muslims who remained in Sanski Most had to sign a loyalty oath to the Serbian authorities? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that the only time in history when someone had to do that was with the Jews in the Second World War. And people did that in order to save their families and their lives. They signed those oaths of loyalty. I signed one myself. Its value was nil. I felt pretty miserable at the time knowing what I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to direct your mind to the second half of June of 1992. Am I right in saying that at this time you and other members of your community requested that Mr. Vrkes come to your community to discuss the prospect of the movement of the Muslim population from your commune?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Obviously, yes. It was through Vladimir Vrkes and some other people I knew. I contacted them and asked them to come to the Podbrijezje local commune and meet with people in order to explain to them how they can safely, quote unquote, move out, leave their homes, because they knew - and I mean both them and their neighbours from the local commune of Podlug - that all of these people used to be their good neighbours, that they were peace-loving people who had previously had good relationships with them. Mr. Vrkes agreed to do that. He came to Podbrijezje together with Mr. Mikan Davidovic, a lawyer, a person who was in charge of emigration affairs. And I believe there was also Milenko Stojinovic, son of Dane Stojinovic. So we held that meeting at the community centre of Podbrijezje, and in a way I chaired it. After that meeting, there was a rally of citizens. Behind the house of the late Teufik -- sorry, late Kamber Teufik, there were 62 of us. And at that rally the Serbs explained what categories of people would be able to apply for papers necessary to leave their Sanski Most municipality. At that rally, I was one of the five citizens nominated to handle this process. We were given the task to collect the identity cards of all those willing to apply, to take their documents to the municipal building and to handle the procedure for each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to direct your mind now to a different event. And it's an event at the end of July, on the 27th of July of 1992. Your father-in-law was a man who at that time was undergoing constant medical treatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of medical treatment was he undergoing?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: He was dependent on regular dialysis treatment. Once in every three days he had to go and receive this dialysis treatment either in Prijedor or in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what happened to him on the 27th of July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly I can. On the 27th of July in the morning my wife and his wife put him in a wheelchair and drove him, Ismet Nalic, the 50 metres from my house to the road, and then an ambulance drove by carrying other patients who also needed dialysis. The driver of that ambulance was Mr. Rajko Kriska, a full-time employee of the Sanski Most health centre. We expected him to come back that same afternoon, but then darkness fell and he hadn't come back. We called this Rajko Kriska to find out, and the truth hit us very hard. He told us that on their way back near Carakovo, three Serb soldiers stopped the ambulance and asked him whether there were any Muslims inside. Rajko said, "Yes, there are." And the soldiers said, "Let them come out." Ill and weak as they were, they had to come out and despite Rajko's efforts to protect them they were taken out at the Carakovo checkpoint and Rajko was threatened that he would share their fate if he tried to resist these men.
